title: Database Scaling and Reliability
description: Database Scaling and Reliability. Interview-first coverage of bottleneck diagnosis, replication, partitioning, backpressure, and recovery.
learningObjectives: Distinguish vertical scaling, read replicas, partitioning, and sharding by the bottleneck they address.
Explain replication lag, failover, consistency, RPO, and RTO.
Design connection pooling, backpressure, timeouts, and retries to protect a database.
Choose partition and shard keys that avoid hotspots and preserve queryability.
Plan safe schema migrations and validate recovery with SLOs.

mentalModel.text: Scaling is a sequence of bottleneck-specific interventions, not a single architecture switch. Measure whether the constraint is CPU, I/O, locks, connections, query shape, or data volume, then choose the smallest change that improves the SLO without breaking consistency or operability.

blocks.text: Vertical scaling adds capacity to one node. Query improvements can be cheaper than new infrastructure. Read replicas distribute eligible reads but do not accelerate a write-bound primary and may serve stale data.

blocks.title: Intervention map
rows: Reduce work, tune queries, right-size capacity

steps.title: Measure SLO
steps.description: Break down latency, throughput, errors, and saturation.

steps.title: Localize constraint
steps.description: Separate query work, lock waits, pool waits, and storage latency.

steps.title: Target one cause
steps.description: Prefer a reversible change tied to evidence.

steps.title: Load-test
steps.description: Use representative data and read/write mix.

blocks.text: A read replica may not yet contain a recent commit. Read-after-write flows may need primary routing or a consistency-aware wait. High availability also needs leader promotion, fencing against split brain, client reconnection, and failover drills.

blocks.title: Recovery objectives
rows: Can the last 5 seconds of writes be lost?
Promote and route to a healthy node
How do clients find the new primary?

blocks.text: A replica is not automatically a backup. Replication can copy accidental deletes or corruption; backups and restore drills protect against different failures.

Partitioning divides a table into manageable pieces within a database system. Sharding distributes data across independent nodes and adds routing, rebalancing, cross-shard query, and transaction challenges. A shard key must balance distribution with common query filters.

blocks.title: Range partition example

blocks.problem: An events table grows by billions of rows and most queries filter by time.
reasoning: Confirm time predicates are consistently present and old data has a retention policy.
Partition by time if pruning and maintenance benefits justify partition count and index overhead.
Do not confuse partitioning inside a database with distributing writes across multiple nodes.
blocks.outcome: Partitioning can improve lifecycle management and pruning; sharding is a separate distribution decision.

blocks.text: Each active connection consumes resources. Pool size is a global budget across app replicas and workers. Timeouts bound waits; backpressure and load shedding prevent unbounded queues. Retries should be bounded, use backoff/jitter, and be safe to repeat.

blocks.title: Connection budget sketch
blocks.source:
total_possible_connections = app_replicas * pool_max_per_replica
reserve capacity for admin, migrations, monitoring, and workers
measure pool wait and DB saturation before increasing limits

blocks.problem: A deployment doubles app replicas and PostgreSQL reports too many connections.
reasoning: Calculate total connections across replicas, workers, and rolling-deployment overlap.
Set a global budget and right-size pools or use a pooling proxy.
Measure pool wait and saturation before changing max_connections.
blocks.outcome: Pool sizing is a global capacity problem; bound concurrency at both application and database boundaries.

blocks.text: Large schema changes can lock tables or compete with live traffic. Expand-and-contract adds backward-compatible schema, deploys compatible code, backfills in batches, switches use, and removes the old form later. Reliability requires tested recovery, not just configured backups.

steps.title: Dual compatibility
steps.description: Deploy code compatible with old and new representations.

steps.title: Backfill
steps.description: Use bounded, restartable batches and monitor locks/lag.

steps.title: Switch
steps.description: Verify parity and route reads to the new representation.

steps.title: Contract
steps.description: Remove old schema after rollback windows close.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Do not scale symptoms
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: More replicas or connections do not fix every bottleneck; first distinguish CPU, I/O, locks, pool waits, and query work.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Test the failure path
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: Measure failover and restore time, replica lag, client retries, and data integrity under realistic conditions.

revisionSheet.text: Scale the measured bottleneck; replicas help eligible reads but not primary write throughput.
Partitioning organizes data within a database; sharding distributes it across nodes.
RPO is tolerable data loss; RTO is recovery duration.
Bound pools, queues, timeouts, and retries; test restores and failovers.

questions.prompt: CPU is low but p99 latency is high and many sessions wait on one inventory row. What should be investigated first?

options.text: Lock contention and the hot-row update path
Read replicas for all writes
Random sharding without query analysis
A much larger connection pool

questions.explanation: Lock waits indicate contention; more concurrent sessions can make it worse.

questions.prompt: A replica is 8 seconds behind. A user writes a profile and immediately reads old data from that replica. Why?

options.text: The replica has not yet applied the recent commit
The primary transaction necessarily rolled back
Replicas always provide linearizable reads
The profile needs a larger B-tree

questions.explanation: Asynchronous replication can lag; read-after-write flows need consistency-aware routing.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes partitioning by time from sharding across nodes?

options.text: Partitioning organizes pieces within a database; sharding distributes data across nodes
Partitioning always adds servers
Sharding has no routing impact
They are identical in all systems

questions.explanation: Partitioning helps pruning/lifecycle; sharding adds distribution and routing complexity.

questions.prompt: There are 20 application replicas, each with pool max 50. What is their configured upper bound before rollout overlap?

options.text: 1,000 connections
70 connections
100 connections
20,050 connections

questions.explanation: 20 multiplied by 50 is 1,000 potential connections, before other workers and reserves.

questions.prompt: A shard key distributes data evenly, but most queries filter by tenant_id and the key is unrelated. What can happen?

options.text: Queries scatter across many shards
Every query becomes local automatically
Rebalancing is eliminated
The database changes the shard key per query

questions.explanation: Distribution alone is insufficient; shard keys should also align with query routing.

questions.prompt: Which distinction between RPO and RTO is correct?

options.text: RPO bounds tolerable data loss; RTO targets service restoration time
RPO is latency and RTO is index size
Both measure replica count
RPO is isolation and RTO is a backup file

questions.explanation: RPO concerns data loss; RTO concerns recovery duration.

questions.prompt: A retry policy immediately retries every failed write forever. During an outage, load increases. What should change?

options.text: Bound retries, add backoff/jitter and idempotency, and apply backpressure
Retry faster and forever
Remove timeouts
Maximize every pool

questions.explanation: Unbounded immediate retries amplify load and can duplicate side effects.

questions.prompt: A costly backfill is needed on a busy table. Which migration approach is safer?

options.text: Expand compatibly, backfill in batches, switch use, then contract later
Lock the table for the entire release
Deploy code requiring the column before adding it
Run one unbounded transaction at peak traffic

questions.explanation: Expand-and-contract separates compatibility, backfill, cutover, and removal.

questions.prompt: Which are valid reasons to introduce a read replica?

options.text: Distribute eligible reads when lag is acceptable
Provide a failover target
Improve read capacity after measuring primary read pressure
Make write throughput unlimited

questions.explanation: Replicas can help reads and availability; writes still flow through the primary.

questions.prompt: Which practices protect a database during overload?

options.text: Bound pool concurrency and queue length
Use deadlines and controlled load shedding
Use bounded retries with backoff and idempotency
Retry indefinitely until recovery

questions.explanation: Bounded concurrency, deadlines, and controlled retries prevent overload amplification.

questions.prompt: A replica is a complete substitute for a backup because deletes and corruption are not replicated.
questions.explanation: Replication often copies deletes and corruption; backups and restore drills cover different failures.

questions.prompt: Increasing a connection pool can worsen latency when the database is already saturated.
questions.explanation: More concurrent queries can increase memory use, lock contention, and queueing without increasing throughput.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A marketplace database is near capacity. Reads are 80% of traffic, some tolerate two seconds of staleness, and writes must remain consistent.
strongAnswerPoints: Measure query shape, CPU/I/O, lock waits, and pool wait first.
Optimize expensive queries and cache stable reads with a freshness contract.
Route only eligible reads to replicas and monitor lag and origin saturation.
pitfalls: Routing every read to replicas without a consistency contract
Change one variable at a time and measure the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would measure the actual bottleneck, optimize expensive queries, cache stable reads, then route only eligible reads to replicas. Read-after-write flows remain on the primary or use consistency-aware routing; I would load-test lag and failover.

interviewScenarios.prompt: Design reliability for a payment service with a 60-second recovery target and near-zero acknowledged-write loss tolerance.
strongAnswerPoints: Translate the business target into explicit RPO/RTO and acknowledgement semantics.
Choose replication/failover and fencing that meet the target, plus independent backups.
Test failover, restore, client reconnection, idempotency, and the runbook.
pitfalls: Claiming asynchronous replication guarantees zero data loss
Change one variable at a time and measure the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would make the RPO/RTO explicit, select a failover design that meets tolerated loss, keep independent backups, and run timed failover and restore drills. Application retries must be idempotent.
